The agent access war has started！

Meta's Muse recently hit #1 on the App Store. But soon Amazon blocked it. Jefferies then found a third of the US shopping and travel sites it tested block it too.

ByteDance is running into the same thing in China. It gave every app 30 days to opt out of its Doubao phone agent. 155 did, including WeChat, Taobao, Alipay, and even DeepSeek and Kimi.

What is this war really about? Data security, privacy, or money? An agent shopping for you doesn't click sponsored listings, while Amazon made ~$68B from ads last year. Tencent and Alibaba, which make up 57% of ByteDance's list, are each pushing their own AI agents.

Shopify let Muse in and Meta is already signing connector deals with Walmart and Best Buy. If access ends up going to whoever pays, do we eventually need some kind of agent neutrality rule? What do you think?

note_tweet.text:
Some observations about the "total" automation of software engineering:

1. There are more software engineers now than in 2025, and demand is growing.

2. Software engineers have never worked harder than they do now.

3. They largely don't write code anymore, agents write ~100% of the code.

4. The bottom line of the companies that employs these engineers and agents (i.e. the terminal purpose of all this code) is typically not budging as a result of AI adoption.

This is why you have to think in terms of systems. Automating one aspect of a system creates its own friction and moves the bottlenecks elsewhere.

Some impressions from the Bank-Fund meetings in Bangkok:

1. The words are all negative but the numbers are all positive. Is all about unprecedented waves of shocks and risks while the IMF upgraded the forecast to something even stronger.

2. No one cares about tariffs anymore, they expect them to continue forever and have adjusted and moved on.

3. Everyone cares a lot about high interest rates. They expect them to continue forever but they haven't moved on.

4. Oil prices fall somewhere between these two. Everyone cares some, aren't sure if they'll continue and have partially moved on.

5. Everyone is having exactly the same conversations about AI as they are having here: will the demand boost continue, is it a bubble, will it kill jobs, when will it show up in productivity. I sensed much more optimism than pessimism and finance ministers and central bankers are not particuarly interested in p(doom).

6. No one seemed to mind that Scott Bessent didn't bother to attend.

note_tweet.text:
A few reflections from travelling (w/ @ed_shackle, @sebwride++) through data-centre country in Michigan/Ohio in my latest for @TheEconomist.

1/ The issue really is moving votes to the Democrats. That's now visible in our polling, too (h/t @OwenWntr), but also in the scale of on-the-ground discontent. I'm quite a bit more bearish on the prospects for big new data-centre projects in blue states after the trip.

2/ I really didn't hear that much direct anti-AI sentiment. The mood much more was a cocktail of worries about local harms (water, electricity bills, house prices), plus a total distrust of businesses and politicians. Against that backdrop, assurances about the water usage of closed-loop cooling systems really don't cut through. And, though developers will doubtless get cannier at this, cash payoffs to communities can easily look like subterfuge and do little to help.

3/ Still, moratoriums are at this stage much more bark than bite (h/t @mayabarkin for the data there). Only about 2GW seems actually delayed. The bigger risk is deterring newer projects, but I'd still guess that affects the exact locations more than whether the build-out happens at all.

4/ The question I'm left with is what comes after data centres as the big AI political issue into next year. A few obvious candidates are: a big cyberattack, the sheer scale of AI-related PAC spending in the 2028 cycle, the early innings of job displacement.

5/ What the data-centre issue should tell us, I think, is that voters' hostility to new technologies that change their lives in unpleasant ways is vast—especially when those changes are less positive-sum than data centres. So, however mad you expect AI as a technology to make the next few years, scale that up accordingly to account for a much more scrambled politics.

Do take a look at my piece on this here: https://t.co/Ha9R8uYF7i
And at our Checks and Balances podcast, where I contributed a short diary featuring lots of conversations with voters https://t.co/XLwgNTWRLs

there are some good provisions in this bill, but ultimately it’s a big step back from the FRONTIER Act. 

ai capabilities are advancing rapidly — it just doesn’t make sense to cement a weaker federal ceiling into place now. 

a few specific areas for improvement:

- create stronger mechanisms to compel corrective action, so major issues auditors identify don’t go unaddressed;

- foster true auditor independence by not allowing auditors to be paid (or selected) by the labs they audit;

- empower the government to establish and iterate on strong minimum standards, so they grow alongside capabilities. 

if you’re going to preempt many state safety laws, the least you can do is create a federal regulatory regime that can evolve in time.
